chunks: And that which was narrated is: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Humayd ibn Ziyad from Ibn Sama'ah from a number of our companions from Aban ibn Uthman from al-Fadl ibn Abd al-Malik, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who had no wealth, so some of his companions financed his pilgrimage; does he fulfill the Hajj of Islam? He said, 'Yes. If he becomes wealthy after that, he must perform Hajj.' I asked, 'Will that Hajj be complete or deficient if he did not perform it from his own wealth?' He said, 'Yes, the Hajj of Islam is fulfilled for him, and it is complete and not deficient. And if he becomes wealthy, let him perform Hajj.'

His saying (peace be upon him), 'And if he becomes wealthy, let him perform Hajj,' is understood as being in the manner of recommendation (istihbab), and the first narration indicates this. And his saying (peace be upon him) in this narration also, 'He has fulfilled the Hajj of Islam, and it is complete and not deficient,' indicates what we mentioned. And what followed of his saying, 'And if he becomes wealthy, let him perform Hajj,' the meaning intended is what we mentioned of recommendation, because when he fulfills the Hajj of Islam, there is nothing after that except recommendation and recommendation. And the one who is poor (mu'sir) when he performs Haj for another, that suffices him for the Hajj of Islam as long as he is not wealthy. So when he becomes wealthy, Hajj becomes obligatory upon him. What indicates this is what was narrated:

key_terms.الْمُعْسِرُ: The one who is poor/financially constrained

ai.seo_question: Does a poor person's Hajj financed by others count as the obligatory Hajj, and what happens if they become rich later?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from al-Fadl ibn Abd al-Malik to clarify that a poor person’s Hajj funded by others fully satisfies the obligatory *Hajj al-Islam* and is deemed complete. The phrase 'if he becomes wealthy, let him perform Hajj' is interpreted by scholars as *istihbab* (recommended) rather than a new *wajib*, distinguishing it from the initial obligation, though some jurists argue for a second obligatory Hajj upon acquiring surplus wealth. This highlights the Shia principle that financial capacity (*istita'ah*) is the condition for obligation, and once fulfilled, the duty is discharged regardless of the source of funds.
